'''John Stanley Gooden''' (11 April 1920 – 9 June 1950) was an Australian physicist. A 1941 graduate of the [[University of Adelaide]], he served during the [[Second World War]] in the Australian Army and with the [[Council for Scientific and Industrial Research]]'s Radiophysics Laboratory at the [[University of Sydney]], where he was involved in the development of [[radar]] and the design of a [[linear particle accelerator]]. After the war he joined [[Mark Oliphant]] at the [[University of Birmingham]], where he worked on the [[proton]] [[synchrotron]].

==Early life and education==
John Stanley Gooden was born in [[Adelaide]], [[South Australia]], on 11 April 1920,<ref name="Nature">{{cite journal |last=Smith |first=W.I.B. |title=Dr. J. S. Gooden |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume=166 |issue=134 |date=22 July 1950 |page=134 |doi=10.1038/166134a0 |bibcode=1950Natur.166..134S }}</ref> the oldest son of Frank Taylor Gooden and his wife Ettie {{nee}} Atkin. He had an older brother, Raymond Frank, and a sister, Margaret Patricia.<ref name="NAA">{{cite web |title=Gooden John Stanley|id=B884, S42308 |via=RecordSearch  |publisher= National Archives of Australia  |url=https://recordsearch.naa.gov.au/SearchNRetrieve/Interface/DetailsReports/ItemDetail.aspx?Barcode=6342223 |access-date=19 October 2025}}</ref><ref name="NAA2">{{cite web |title=Leonard Ulysses Hibbard|id=A6119, 586 |via=RecordSearch  |publisher= National Archives of Australia  |url=https://recordsearch.naa.gov.au/SearchNRetrieve/Interface/DetailsReports/ItemDetail.aspx?Barcode=8334542 |access-date=19 October 2025}}</ref> He was educated at [[Pulteney Grammar School]] and later [[St Peter's College, Adelaide|St Peter's College]] in Adelaide, after winning a scholarship to there. He entered the [[University of Adelaide]] in 1938 and won the David Maurray scholarship in 1940, majoring in physics.<ref name="Nature" /><ref>{{cite news |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article74463346 |title=Brilliant Science Student |newspaper=[[The Advertiser (Adelaide)]] |location=South Australia |date=6 December 1940 |access-date=20 October 2025 |page=23 |via=National Library of Australia}}</ref> He played on the university [[lacrosse]] and [[cricket]] teams, and was a lightweight [[boxing|boxer]].<ref name="Nature" /> He was among a group of students who threw [[Max Harris (poet)|Max Harris]] into the [[River Torrens]].<ref name="NAA2" /> He wrote his honours thesis on the detection of ultra-short radio waves, an important means of communication at the time. He also worked with [[John Raymond Wilton]] on a paper on [[functions of a complex variable]] and on three papers with [[Hans Schwerdtfeger]] on [[mechanics]] and [[matrix calculus]].<ref name="CSIRO">{{cite journal |first=Brett A. |last=Gooden |title=John Gooden and the Birmingham Proton Synchrotron |journal=Historical Records of Australian Science |year=2020 |volume=32 |issue=2 |pages=141–155 |doi=10.1071/hr20008 }}</ref> He graduated with his [[Bachelor of Science]] degree with first class honours in November 1941.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article45740018 |title=University Of Adelaide |newspaper=[[The Advertiser (Adelaide)]] |volume=LXXXIV |issue=25942 |location=South Australia |date=26 November 1941 |access-date=20 October 2025 |page=5 |via=National Library of Australia}}</ref>

==Second World War==
While at the University of Adelaide, Gooden was called up for national service due to the [[Second World War]] on 8 November 1940, but his enlistment was deferred until after graduation. He was called to active duty on 6 February 1942, with the [[service number]] S42308. He was immediately promoted to [[corporal]] and then [[staff sergeant]] in the [[Royal Australian Army Ordnance Corps|Australian Army Ordnance Corps]] before being commissioned as a [[lieutenant]] on 14 May, and was assigned to the Eastern Command Ordnance Workshops in Sydney.<ref name="NAA" /> On 29 August, he married Claire Ward, the daughter of J.F. Ward, the headmaster of [[Prince Alfred College]] in Adelaide, in a ceremony at the [[Wesley College, University of Sydney|Wesley College]] chapel at the [[University of Sydney]] officiated by Reverend Leslie Bennett, the master of the college. They had one child, a son.<ref name="Nature" /><ref>{{cite news |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article48880666 |title=Items of Interest |newspaper=[[The Advertiser (Adelaide)]] |volume=LXXXV |issue=26177 |location=South Australia |date=28 August 1942 |access-date=20 October 2025 |page=5 |via=National Library of Australia}}</ref> Gooden was admitted to the [[Concord Repatriation General Hospital|113th General Hospital]] for renal investigation on 6 November 1942 and discharged on 25 November.<ref name="NAA"/> He was diagnosed with chronic [[nephritis]] and discharged from the Army on medical grounds.<ref name="CSIRO"/> He was placed on the retired list on 7 December.<ref name="NAA"/>

Gooden then joined the [[Council for Scientific and Industrial Research]]'s Radiophysics Laboratory at the University of Sydney, where he worked under [[Joseph L. Pawsey]] in examining the factors involved in producing ultra-short-wave radio transmission using a high-powered [[cavity magnetron]]. Although this had already been studied overseas, little information was available in Australia. Gooden was given a [[Type 271 radar]] to study. A 10&nbsp;cm radar unit was constructed by the Radiophysics Laboratory based on its CV56 cavity magnetron and was used to equip [[Royal Australian Navy]] ships. The work formed the basis of his [[Master of Science]] thesis. He was awarded the degree by the University of Adelaide in December 1945.<ref name="CSIRO"/><ref>{{cite thesis |title=Coaxial-waveguide transformer: impedance properties, specified in W-plane, field properties and application to the design of a magnetron output transformer |degree=MSc |date=1945 |last=Gooden |first=John Stanley |publisher=University of Adelaide |location=Adelaide |hdl=2440/122177 }}</ref> In early 1945, [[Edward George Bowen|Edward George "Taffy" Bowen]] asked Gooden to design a low-voltage [[linear particle accelerator]]. By April, the design had progressed to the point where Bowen decided to build it. When the accelerator ran in September 1945, it produced an output of 1 million [[electronvolt]]s (1 Mev).<ref name="CSIRO"/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bowen |first1=E. G. |author-link=Edward George Bowen |last2=Pulley |first2=O. O. |last3=Gooden |first3=J. S.|date=June 1946 |title=Application of pulse technique to the acceleration of elementary particles |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume=157 |issue=3,999 |page=840 |doi=10.1038/157840A0 |bibcode=1946Natur.157..840B }}</ref>

==Post-war==
On 14 March 1945, Gooden wrote to [[Mark Oliphant]] at the [[University of Birmingham]] in England asking if he could be admitted to study there. Oliphant offered him a three-year Nuffield Research Fellowship to work on his doctorate. Bowen wrote letters of introduction for Gooden to [[Robert Watson-Watt]] and [[Edward Appleton]] in which he described Gooden as "one of the best young physicists to have come out of Australia during the war".<ref name="CSIRO"/> Accompanied by his wife Claire, Gooden left for the UK on the troopship {{ship|RMMV|Stirling Castle||6}} on 14 November.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article48680305 |title=S.A. Scientist For Atomic Research |newspaper=[[The Advertiser (Adelaide)]] |volume=88 |issue=27197 |location=South Australia |date=4 December 1945 |access-date=20 October 2025 |page=4 |via=National Library of Australia}}</ref> The project that Oliphant set Gooden to work on was the design of a 1 Gev [[proton]] [[synchrotron]].<ref name="CSIRO"/> [[Edwin McMillan]] (in the United States) and [[Vladimir Veksler]] (in the Soviet Union) had independently come up with the concept, but Oliphant went one better than them by proceeding to actually build one.<ref>{{cite thesis |last=Ellyard |first=David |degree=PhD |location=Sydney |publisher=University of New South Wales |title=Mark Oliphant FRS and the Birmingham Proton Synchrotron |url=https://unsworks.unsw.edu.au/server/api/core/bitstreams/48908c25-9a20-48c4-9346-a21b236d8fd2/content |access-date=20 October 2025 |pages=21–25}}</ref> The proton synchrotron design formed the basis of Gooden' [[Doctor of Philosophy]] (PhD) thesis.<ref>{{cite thesis |last=Gooden |first=John Stanley |degree=PhD |date=1948 |publisher=University of Birmingham |title=The Proton Synchrotron |url= https://birmingham.primo.exlibrisgroup.com/permalink/44BIR_INST/jmfpgg/alma990031369090204871  |access-date=20 October 2025 }}</ref>

That year, the Birmingham team published two papers on the on it,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gooden |first1=J. S. |last2=Jensen |first2=H. H. |last3=Symonds, J. L. |year=1947 |title=Theory of the Proton Synchrotron |journal=Proceedings of the Physical Society |volume=59 |issue=4 |pages=677–693 |doi=10.1088/0959-5309/59/4/315 |bibcode=1947PPS....59..677G }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Oliphant |first1=M. L. |author-link1=Mark Oliphant |last2=Gooden |first2=J. S. |last3=Hide |first3=G. S. |year=1947 |title=The Acceleration of Charged Particles to Very High Energies |journal=Proceedings of the Physical Society |volume=59 |issue=4 |pages=666–677 |doi=10.1088/0959-5309/59/4/314 |bibcode=1947PPS....59..666O }}</ref> and Oliphant sent  Gooden and [[John H. Fremlin]] to the United States to see the progress of work on accelerators there. They arrived at the [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory|Radiation Laboratory]] at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], on 3 November, and were shown the {{convert|184|in|cm|adj=on}} [[cyclotron]]. In turn, they briefed [[Ernest Lawrence]], Edwin McMillan and [[Robert Serber]] on their work in Birmingham. Returning eastward, they met with [[Robert R. Wilson]] at [[Cornell University]] and toured the [[General Electric Research Laboratory]] at [[Schenectady]], where they had a 70 Mev synchrotron in operation.<ref name="CSIRO"/><ref>{{cite journal |first=Herbert C. |last=Pollock |title=The Discovery of Synchrotron Radiation |journal=[[American Journal of Physics]] |date=1 March 1983 |volume=51 |issue=3 |pages=278–280 |doi=10.1119/1.13289 |bibcode=1983AmJPh..51..278P }}</ref> Finally, they met with [[M. Stanley Livingston]] and [[Richard Q. Twiss]] at the [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]], where they received input on their design. The development of the synchrotron had prompted Livingston to drop his plans to build a cyclotron and to build a synchrotron instead.<ref name="CSIRO"/>

Gooden's PhD was conferred on him by [[Anthony Eden]], the [[Chancellor of the University of Birmingham]], on 3 July 1948. On 3 August, he accepted an offer of a research stipend of a £750 ({{Inflation|AU|1500|1948|fmt=eq|r=-3|cursign=AUD$}}) at the new [[Australian National University]] (ANU) in [[Canberra]], where Oliphant had also accepted a position. Although the Birmingham proton synchrotron had priority, Oliphant wanted Gooden to make a start on the design of a proton accelerator for the ANU. That building one in Australia would be even more difficult than the construction of the Birmingham accelerator in the scarcities of post-war Britain was not overlooked; to work around this, Oliphant proposed to use a cyclotron to accelerate protons to around 250 Mev and then feed them into a synchrotron. Gooden counter-proposed building a 500 Mev synchrotron that could be built in 12 to 18 months for £20,000 ({{Inflation|AU|40000|1948|fmt=eq|r=-6|cursign=AUD$}}) but Oliphant rejected the idea. But with the [[Bevatron]] under construction at Berkeley planned to produce 3 Gev and the [[Cosmotron]] at Brookhaven projected to produce 6 Gev, it seemed likely that Oliphant's cyclosynchrotron would be obsolete before it was built.<ref name="CSIRO"/><ref>{{cite journal |last=Oliphant |first=M. L. |author-link=Mark Oliphant |year=1950b |title=The Cyclosynchrotron |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume=165 |issue=4195 |pages=466–468 |doi=10.1038/165466A0 |bibcode=1950Natur.165..466O }}</ref>

==Death==
By Match 1950, Gooden was showing signs of being increasingly unwell. The mercury used in the Birmingham proton synchrotron may have aggravated his nephritis. In May Gooden, his wife Claire and his young son were flown back to Australia at the ANU's expense.<ref name="CSIRO"/><ref>{{cite book |last1=Cockburn |first1=Stewart |author-link1=Stewart Cockburn |first2=David |last2=Ellyard |title=Oliphant: The Life and Times of Sir Mark Oliphant |location = Adelaide |year=1981 |publisher=Axiom Books |isbn=978-0-9594164-0-4 |oclc=8666832 |page=229 }}</ref> Gooden died at [[Wakefield Street Private Hospital]] in Adelaide on 9 June 1950.<ref name="Trove">{{cite news |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article44939389 |title=Brilliant S.A. Physicist Dead At 30 |newspaper=[[The Advertiser (Adelaide)]]  |volume=92 |issue=28,601  |location=South Australia |date=10 June 1950 |access-date=19 October 2025 |page=2 |via=National Library of Australia}}</ref><ref name="NYT">{{cite news |title=Dr. John Stanley Gooden |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=10 June 1950 |page=17 |url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1950/06/10/113156748.html?pageNumber=17 |access-date=19 October 2025}}</ref> He was buried in [[Mitcham Cemetery|Mitcham Anglican Cemetery]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Mitcham Anglican Cemetery Index |website=www.ozgenonline.com |url=http://www.ozgenonline.com/~forever_remembered/mitcham.htm |access-date=21 October 2025}}</ref>
